title: Reliability, Measurement Error, and Diagnostic Performance of the King-Devick Test in a Women’s Flat-Track Roller Derby and Rugby League: A Four-Season Cohort Study
content: Background: The King-Devick Test (KDT) is widely used as an adjunct to concussion assessment, yet its measurement properties and diagnostic performance in female athletes from understudied contact sports remain unclear. Purpose: To evaluate the reliability, measurement error, and diagnostic performance of the KDT in women's flat-track roller derby (WFTRD) and women's rugby league (WRL). Study Design: Retrospective cohort study with an exploratory diagnostic comparison against same-day retest pseudo-controls. Methods: Data from 388 preseason baseline assessments (225 WFTRD, 163 WRL) and 52 clinician-diagnosed concussions were analysed across four seasons (2023-2026). Test-retest reliability was assessed using ICC(2,1), standard error of measurement (SEM), and minimal detectable change (MDC). Exploratory discrimination of clinician-confirmed concussion observations from same-day preseason retest variability was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis and worsening thresholds. Results: The KDT demonstrated good test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.83), with similar performance across sports. A consistent practice effect was observed, with second baseline trials completed 2.52 s faster than first trials. The SEM was 3.98 s, corresponding to MDC values of 9.26-11.03 s. An exploratory, data-derived threshold for concussion identification (worsening ≥0.93 s) yielded 92.3% sensitivity (95% CI 81.8-97.0%) and 82.1% specificity (95% CI 77.7-85.9%) relative to same-day preseason retest observations, with a negative likelihood ratio of 0.09. Any worsening from baseline identified all concussion cases but reduced specificity. Continuous KDT worsening discriminated clinician-confirmed concussion cases from same-day preseason retest observations (AUC = 0.917); however, this estimate is exploratory and may be optimistic given the comparator group. In contrast, MDC-derived thresholds demonstrated high specificity but poor sensitivity. Conclusion: The KDT showed good same-day reliability and strong exploratory discrimination between clinician-confirmed concussion observations and same-day retest variability, although diagnostic accuracy estimates should be interpreted cautiously given the comparator group. Small declines from baseline were observed in most confirmed concussion events among athletes removed from play for suspected concussion. The KDT may be a valuable adjunct to multimodal concussion assessment but should not be used in isolation for diagnosis.
